correctness.rationale: All 18 branch choices are covered by strict feasibility exclusions or a quantitative two-row Gram bound. Hub-singleton/leaf-singleton/other-global exists exactly while a+h<1, with top Gram eigenvalue A(h); all other feasible choices have squared norm <=H(h)=2-4h+6h^2. Both optimal branches have explicit strictly positive open-cell witnesses and right singular perturbations; tie cells are controlled by segmentwise piecewise linearity. Coordinate modulus reduction establishes the inequality for complex signals. The standard-library checker constructs and tests the actual branches at 11 parameters and 110000 input cases; numerical experiments do not replace the proof.

originality.rationale: The exact claim is a two-input vertex-Euclidean-to-edge-quadratic Lipschitz norm on the three-vertex path for every fractional exponent, including a nontrivial interior jump. The inspected closest papers establish one-input variation or ordinary-maximal bounds; their statements do not imply the nonlinear two-input fractional norm. Indexed public comparisons and recoverable prior mathematical claims show neither an equivalent statement nor a stronger theorem covering this specific three-scale parameter profile. Risk of unindexed prior work is retained.
residual_risks: Semantic indexing and accessible literature cannot exclude an unindexed equivalent two-input theorem.
The indexed public comparison records did not expose their full manuscripts through the attempted GitHub page fetch; assessment of those records is limited to their published abstracts/summaries.
The small-graph finite-cell method could conceivably be implicit in a stronger nonlinear Lipschitz principle not identified by the focused searches.

value.rationale: This is a complete natural noncomplete graph fractional perturbation invariant across an entire exponent interval, with a genuine interior discontinuity at the collision of singleton and whole-ball feasibility, rather than an arbitrary finite numerical case. The sharp threshold and jump distinguish stability of nonlinear input differences from known one-input smoothing estimates and motivate investigations of active-cell collapse on other graphs.
